About me

Where simulation meets the shop floor

As a senior mechanical engineering student at Anderson University, I thrive at the intersection of rigorous analytical modeling and hands-on physical realization. My engineering journey is anchored by a deep-seated curiosity for how things work and a commitment to designing systems that are efficient, reliable, and practically deployable on the shop floor.

My technical “Aha!” moment came during hands-on machine shop fabrication and FEA coursework, where I realized the vital bridge between digital simulation and real-world manufacturing constraints. Studying computer-aided design (SolidWorks), structural FEA (Ansys), and computer numerical control (CNC) machining taught me that a theoretical design is only as good as its manufacturability. This realization transformed how I approach engineering problems: I no longer just design components; I design for tolerance, assembly, safety, and operational longevity.

Through my academic projects and industry collaboration, I have focused on solving tangible mechanical and material handling challenges. Most notably, I am partnering with industrial manufacturers like Dodge Industrial to develop universal material retrieval systems for densely stored vertical bar stock, optimizing space, safety, and workflow efficiency. My practical toolkit includes 3-axis CNC programming with G-code, structural simulation, rapid prototyping, and hybrid project management frameworks.

Beyond technical design, I am driven by servant leadership, collaboration, and ethical responsibility. Whether serving as a project teammate, mentoring peers through complex mechanical analyses, or integrating human-centric values into engineering design, I strive to lead academic groups and extracurricular clubs with empathy, integrity, and diligence. I am eager to transition from academia into an engineering career where I can contribute to innovative manufacturing solutions and mechanical systems that improve operations and serve communities well.

Computer-Aided Simulation & Modeling · Anderson University

Does the simulation match reality?

Engineering projects where I build a digital model, run the numbers, and then put the real thing on a testing machine to check my work.

Project 01 · Structural

Maple Dining Table: SolidWorks, Ansys & a Real Replica

I modeled a full-scale maple dining table and asked one question: when 200 lbf is applied to the center of the tabletop, how accurately do the simulations predict how much it bends? I validated SolidWorks against a 1:10 physical replica tested on an Instron machine, with Ansys as a further comparison.

10.16%Error between SolidWorks and the physical test
0.0482 inSimulated center deflection at 2.0 lbf
0.0531 inMeasured center deflection at 2.0 lbf
~99.8 lbfPeak load before replica failure

Simulated vs. measured deflection

SolidWorks FEA: 0.0482 in
Instron test: 0.0531 in

The replica deflected 0.0049 in more than the model, which falls inside the 10–15% validation target I set in my project proposal.

The real table

1 · The digital model

A SolidWorks sub-assembly of the tabletop, supports, dovetail joints and 1.5 in pegs, plus a steel loading cylinder. Maple was defined as a linear elastic isotropic material.

E = 9,790.56 MPaν = 0.434Yield 28.27 MPa

2 · The replica

Built at 1:10 scale from plywood, particleboard, pine and dowels. The dovetails were simplified to a glued slot cut to a trapezoid. Scaled load: 2.0 lbf (200 lbf × 0.10²).

Plywood topPine supportDowel pegs

3 · The real test

An Instron 34TM-50 drove a ~0.4 in steel cylinder into the center of the replica, logging force and displacement through the linear range until the replica failed.

Instron 34TM-5080 kN load cell

The 1:10 replica and the Instron test

Simulation results

Ansys Discovery simulation of the full table

I ran the same load cases in Ansys Discovery, in the same order as the SolidWorks studies. Setup: Maple wood, gravity, four fixed supports at the leg bases, bonded contacts between parts (the Ansys default), and an 890 N (about 200 lbf) distributed force.

Why the model and the replica disagree

  • The replica needed a small seating take-up (~0.045 in) as the supports settled onto the steel anvils.
  • The CAD supports are fully fixed; the real ones can rotate and slip slightly.
  • Hand-fitted joints, glue, and wood indentation under the small cylinder add compliance.
  • The model assumes perfectly uniform, isotropic maple; real wood has grain and knots.
Project 02 · Thermal & Multiphysics

Raspberry Pi 4: Assembly Analysis in Ansys Discovery

I brought a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B CAD model from SolidWorks into Ansys Discovery and assigned realistic materials to its 170 solid bodies, the groundwork for a thermal study of how the board handles heat.

Material assignments

MaterialApplied to
PCB laminate (epoxy/glass fiber)The board itself
Brass C37700GPIO header pins and the audio jack
Stainless steel 316USB and Ethernet housings
Silicon, pureProcessor and memory chips
Glass, soda limeSelected components
Copper, pure (hard)Connectors and small components

Inside Ansys Discovery

The thermal study

The goal: heat the three main integrated circuits on the board to 150 °F (65.56 °C) and watch how that heat spreads through the whole circuit board until it reaches thermal equilibrium.

Boundary conditions
  • Three main ICs held at 150 °F (65.56 °C)
  • Ambient air temperature and natural convection on exposed surfaces
  • Bonded contacts so heat conducts between bodies
  • Material properties from the table above
Deliverables
  • Color-coded temperature map at equilibrium
  • Animation of the full board warming from ambient to equilibrium
  • A documented list of every thermal condition set manually or by Ansys
